title: Every art aims at some good
src: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.1 · tr. D. P. Chase (1847)
author: Aristotle
lines: Every art, and every science reduced to a teachable form,
and in like manner every action and moral choice,
aims, it is thought, at some good:
for which reason a common and by no means a bad description of the Chief Good is,
why: The first sentence of Aristotle's Ethics, and the question behind everything he wrote: what is it for? Whatever you do this morning, you do for the sake of something, and that for the sake of something else. Aristotle asks where the chain ends. Say it when you are busy and have forgotten why.

title: Didn't one fashion us in the womb?
author: Job
lines: If I have despised the cause of my male servant
what then will I do when God rises up?
When he visits, what will I answer him?
Didn’t he who made me in the womb make him?
Didn’t one fashion us in the womb?
why: Job, a rich man with servants, says that his servants had a right to argue their case against him, because the same God made master and servant in the same way. It is one of the oldest answers to the idea that some people are born to serve. Say it when you are tempted to think anyone beneath you.

title: Face to face
author: Paul the Apostle
lines: For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face.
but then I will know fully,
even as I was also fully known.
why: Aristotle thought the happiest life was spent thinking about what is highest. Paul agrees that we were made to know, and admits we only know in part. But he promises more than thought: to see face to face, and to find that we were known all along. Say it when you cannot see the point of things.
